blocks.text: 1. Batches

blocks.alt: A dataset splits into batches, processed one at a time

blocks.text: Epochs, the previous topic, covered one complete pass through the entire training dataset. Batches cover how the training dataset gets divided up within each individual epoch, a genuinely essential practical detail.
A batch is a smaller group of examples, processed one group at a time, rather than processing the entire dataset or a single example at a time, covered in full depth throughout this topic.
2. Why Not Process The Whole Dataset At Once

blocks.alt: The entire dataset at once needs too much memory

blocks.text: This connects back to Batch Gradient Descent, already covered in the Backpropagation & Optimization module. Processing the entire dataset at once for every single update is genuinely expensive, and genuinely slow to see any improvement.
Every single weight update would require a full pass over potentially millions of examples, an approach already covered as impractical at real scale in that earlier topic.
3. Why Not Process One Example At A Time

blocks.alt: One example at a time is too slow with a noisy path

blocks.text: This connects back to Stochastic Gradient Descent, already covered in its own topic. Processing exactly one example at a time is genuinely fast per update, but genuinely noisy, unstable gradient estimates result.

A single example rarely represents the full dataset well, so updates based on just one example at a time can genuinely bounce around rather than converging smoothly, already covered as a real tradeoff in that earlier topic.

blocks.text: 4. The Practical Middle Ground

This connects back to Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, already covered in the Backpropagation & Optimization module. A batch is a genuinely practical middle ground between the two extremes already covered in the previous two sections.
Neither the whole dataset nor a single example, but a small, manageable group, combining reasonably stable gradient estimates with reasonably fast, frequent updates.
5. How Batches Actually Form

blocks.alt: A dataset gets shuffled, then sliced into batches

blocks.text: The genuinely mechanical process of forming batches starts by shuffling the training dataset at the start of each epoch, already covered in the previous topic, before splitting anything up at all.
The shuffled data then gets split into consecutive, equally sized groups, each becoming one individual batch that will be processed in turn throughout that epoch.
6. Why Shuffling Genuinely Matters

blocks.alt: Unshuffled data produces biased, repetitive batches

blocks.text: A genuinely important detail explains why shuffling happens at all. Without shuffling, batches would contain the exact same examples in the exact same order every single epoch, a genuinely real, practical risk.

The network could genuinely learn spurious patterns tied to that fixed ordering, rather than the genuine underlying patterns in the data itself, exactly the kind of unwanted memorization already covered as overfitting in its own topic.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: Forgetting to reshuffle at the start of every epoch, already covered in this topic, is a genuinely common, real implementation mistake. Most established training frameworks handle this automatically, but it is worth verifying.

blocks.text: 7. One Batch, One Update

blocks.alt: One batch produces one gradient step

blocks.text: This connects back to the update rule already covered in Gradient Descent. Processing one batch produces exactly one weight update, computed from that batch's own average gradient across its examples.
This confirms the epoch-versus-updates relationship already covered in the previous topic, where one epoch contains as many individual updates as there are batches within it.
8. The Last Batch Edge Case
A genuinely common, practical edge case arises because the dataset size does not always divide evenly by the batch size, a genuinely mundane but real detail worth understanding.
The final batch in an epoch can genuinely be smaller than all the others, since whatever examples remain after forming full-sized batches simply form one smaller, final batch instead.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing How Batches Connect To The Rest Of Training

This connects back to Batch Normalization, already covered in the Normalization Techniques module. Its own statistics, already covered there, are computed directly from each individual batch already covered throughout this topic.

This connects to memory constraints too, a genuinely real, practical hardware limit. Batches let genuinely large datasets be processed without needing to fit entirely in memory at once, a real, practical necessity at scale.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates shuffling and splitting a small dataset into batches, illustrating the mechanical process already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
dataset_size = 23  # deliberately not evenly divisible by the batch size below
batch_size = 5      # covered further in the next topic

indices = np.arange(dataset_size)
rng.shuffle(indices)  # already covered as why shuffling genuinely matters in this topic

batches = [indices[i:i + batch_size] for i in range(0, dataset_size, batch_size)]

for i, batch in enumerate(batches):
    print(f"Batch {i + 1}: {len(batch)} examples -> indices {batch}")

print(f"\nTotal batches this epoch: {len(batches)}")
print(f"Last batch size: {len(batches[-1])}, smaller than the rest, already covered as the last batch edge case in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows 5 batches of size 5 followed by one final batch of size 3, exactly the last batch edge case already covered in this topic, since 23 does not divide evenly by 5.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A batch is a smaller group of training examples processed together for a single weight update.
Batches offer a practical middle ground between processing the whole dataset at once and one example at a time.
Each epoch shuffles the dataset, then splits it into consecutive batches.
Shuffling prevents the network from learning spurious patterns tied to a fixed example ordering.
Processing one batch produces exactly one weight update.
The final batch in an epoch can be smaller than the rest when the dataset size does not divide evenly.
Batch Normalization computes its statistics directly from each individual batch.
Batches also make it possible to train on datasets too large to fit entirely in memory at once.
Next up: Batch Size, the specific hyperparameter controlling how many examples go into each batch.
